summary: Updates BGP so that messages may be larger than the 4,096 octets allowed by RFC 4271. The new maximum is 65,535 octets for all messages except OPEN and KEEPALIVE. This is needed as BGP gains new address families and features that need more room.

eli5.summary: A small envelope can only fit so many pages. As more news needed to be sent, this made the envelope bigger so routers can write longer letters to each other.

subtitle: Lets BGP routers exchange messages up to 65,535 octets instead of 4,096, once both sides agree.

tldr.problem: RFC 4271 caps every BGP message at 4,096 octets, which is too small as BGP gains new address families and features such as BGPsec and BGP-LS.
tldr.mechanism: A new BGP capability (code 6, length 0) lets a speaker say it can receive Extended Messages. Once a peer has advertised it, the other side may send UPDATE-style messages up to 65,535 octets. OPEN and KEEPALIVE keep the old limit.
tldr.outcome: Large messages are only allowed between peers that both opted in, and a speaker must shrink or withhold oversized UPDATEs headed for peers that did not. The RFC updates RFC 4271.

today: RFC 8654 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2019 that updates RFC 4271. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why 4,096 Octets Is Not Enough
sections.content:
RFC 4271 requires a maximum BGP message size of 4,096 octets. As BGP is extended to carry new address families (AFIs), subsequent address families (SAFIs) and other features, for example BGPsec (RFC 8205) and BGP-LS (RFC 7752), that limit becomes too small.

This RFC extends the limit from 4,096 octets to 65,535 octets for all messages except OPEN and KEEPALIVE. A message longer than 4,096 octets is called a BGP Extended Message.
sections.eli5: BGP routers talk using messages, and the old rule said a message could not be longer than one small page. As routers had more to say, one page was not enough.

sections.title: The Extended Message Capability
sections.content:
Support is announced with a new BGP capability, the BGP Extended Message Capability, defined with Capability Code 6 and Capability Length 0. A speaker advertises it using the Capabilities Advertisement mechanism of RFC 5492. Advertising it tells the peer that the speaker can receive and properly handle Extended Messages.

A speaker that can receive Extended Messages SHOULD advertise the capability. It MAY send Extended Messages to a peer only if it received the capability from that peer. Anyone who advertises it MUST be able to receive a message up to and including 65,535 octets. Peers that want to use it MUST also support the UPDATE error handling of RFC 7606.
sections.eli5: Before sending a long letter, a router checks that the other router has said, 'I can read long letters.' If it has not said so, the router sticks to short letters.

sections.title: Sending and Propagating Large Messages
sections.content:
The capability applies to all messages except OPEN and KEEPALIVE; these exceptions reduce the complexity of backward compatibility. The smallest message is still a KEEPALIVE of 19 octets. Applications that put information into BGP messages MUST limit their payload with the maximum message size in mind.

An UPDATE usually spreads across many networks, including to speakers that do not support Extended Messages, so an announcement whose attribute set plus NLRI exceeds 4,096 octets may cause lack of reachability. When a speaker must pass such an UPDATE on to a neighbor that has not advertised the capability, it SHOULD first try to shrink it by removing attributes eligible under the 'attribute discard' approach of RFC 7606. If it is still too big, it must not be sent, and if that prefix was advertised to the peer before, it must be withdrawn.

Inside an AS, a consistent external view can only be guaranteed if all iBGP speakers advertise the capability. Otherwise the operator should consider whether to advertise it to external peers, and should monitor dropped routes and discarded attributes during rollout.
sections.eli5: If a long letter has to pass through a router that can only read short ones, the sender first crosses out the unimportant lines. If it is still too long, it is not sent at all.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
A speaker that could use Extended Messages but did not advertise the capability, for example because of configuration, MUST NOT accept one, and MUST NOT adopt a more liberal policy. A listener that has not advertised the capability and receives a message longer than 4,096 octets generates a NOTIFICATION with the error subcode Bad Message Length.

UPDATE error handling from Section 6.3 of RFC 4271 is unchanged. However, a NOTIFICATION sent to a speaker that has not advertised the capability MUST NOT exceed 4,096 octets.

The RFC also recommends that implementers be conservative in using Extended Messages, and requires future protocol specifications to say how to handle peers that can only take 4,096-octet messages.
sections.eli5: If a router did not say it could read long letters, it must refuse them, and any complaint sent back to it has to stay short too.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 4271
sections.content:
RFC 4271 says the value of the Length field MUST always be at least 19 and no greater than 4096. This document changes the upper number to 65,535 for all messages except OPEN and KEEPALIVE.

Likewise, Section 6.1 of RFC 4271 requires an error when a message is over 4,096 octets. For every message except OPEN and KEEPALIVE, that limit rises to 65,535 when the receiver has advertised the capability. IANA assigned value 6, 'BGP Extended Message', in the Capability Codes registry.
sections.eli5: The old rulebook said 'no longer than one page'. This RFC adds a note: 'unless both sides agreed to longer ones'.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension does not change BGP's underlying security issues (see RFC 4272). Because larger messages need more buffer memory, there may be more exposure to resource exhaustion, intentional or not.

If a remote speaker crafts a large message on a path where some peers lack support, a speaker that shrinks the message by discarding attributes could break something a peer expected, or enable a downgrade attack, which would only affect the attacker's own message. Reformatting large messages also costs processing. The discardable attributes must have no effect on route selection or installation.
sections.eli5: Bigger letters need bigger mailboxes, so someone could try to flood a router with huge letters. Cutting down a letter on its way can also drop a detail someone was waiting for.
